findings.title: readBytes() allocates an attacker-declared length (up to ~2 GiB) before reading any data
findings.impact: Remote, pre-authentication memory-exhaustion DoS of the client JVM at essentially zero cost to the attacker. A rogue endpoint on the AMQP port, a compromised broker, or an on-path attacker on a plaintext (amqp://) connection sends ~5 bytes and forces a 2 GiB heap allocation, repeatable per connection. Because the array is allocated before any payload byte is consumed, the attacker never has to send the data it claims to be sending: the amplification factor is ~400,000,000x. Reachable before credentials are exchanged, via the longstr fields of Connection.Start (mechanisms, locales) and Connection.Secure (challenge), which are decoded by this class during the handshake while frame-max is still untuned.
findings.evidence: readBytes() does `final long contentLength = unsignedExtend(in.readInt());` (line 86) and then, for any value below Integer.MAX_VALUE, `final byte [] buffer = new byte[(int)contentLength];` (line 88) BEFORE `in.readFully(buffer)` (line 89). The only bound on contentLength is the `< Integer.MAX_VALUE` guard on line 87 — nothing compares it to the negotiated frame maximum, to a configured ceiling, or to the bytes actually remaining. Wrapping the stream in TruncatedInputStream (lines 146-147, 241-242) limits how much can be READ, not how much is ALLOCATED, so the same trick works for every 'S' (line 163) and 'x' (line 211) field inside a field table or array.
findings.recommendation: Validate before allocating: reject contentLength greater than a bound derived from the negotiated frame maximum (or a configurable ceiling) with a MalformedFrameException, and/or read into a growing buffer in bounded chunks so heap use stays proportional to bytes actually received rather than to bytes merely claimed.

findings.title: Unbounded nesting depth in field-table / field-array decoding leads to StackOverflowError
findings.impact: A remote peer crashes the connection's frame-reading thread with a small crafted frame, and the failure mode is an Error rather than a protocol exception, so it escapes the library's IOException-based shutdown path. Unlike F-001 this survives broker re-encoding: a deeply nested header table published by any low-privilege producer is parsed and re-serialised faithfully by the broker and then decoded by every Java consumer that touches the message headers, turning a publish right into a denial of service against other tenants' consumers. Also reachable pre-authentication through the server-properties table of Connection.Start.
findings.evidence: readFieldValue() case 'F' calls readTable() (line 181) and case 'A' calls readArray() (line 184); readTable() calls readFieldValue() (line 150) and readArray() calls readFieldValue() (line 245). The cycle has no depth counter, no recursion limit and no cap on total decoded elements. Each nesting level costs 5 bytes on the wire ('A' plus a 4-byte length), so roughly 50 KB of payload buys ~10,000 stack frames — comfortably inside a default 131072-byte frame-max, and unbounded during the handshake before frame-max is negotiated. Each level also allocates a TruncatedInputStream and a DataInputStream that stay live for the whole descent.
findings.recommendation: Thread an explicit depth argument through readFieldValue/readTable/readArray and throw MalformedFrameException past a small fixed maximum (the AMQP 0-9-1 field-table grammar needs only a handful of levels in practice), or rewrite the descent iteratively with an explicit stack. Consider also capping the total number of decoded fields per frame.

findings.title: Decoder throws an unchecked UnsupportedOperationException on attacker-controlled input
findings.impact: A remote peer chooses which exception type comes out of the frame decoder. A length of 0x7FFFFFFF or above yields a RuntimeException instead of the MalformedFrameException/IOException that every caller of this class is written to expect, so the failure bypasses the protocol-error handling path and can kill a reader or dispatch thread through the generic-Throwable route instead of a clean connection shutdown.
findings.evidence: readBytes() line 91-93: `} else { throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Very long byte vectors and strings not currently supported"); }`. UnsupportedOperationException is unchecked, whereas the sibling error path for a bad type code (line 217) correctly throws MalformedFrameException, which is an IOException. Both are triggered purely by bytes off the wire.
findings.recommendation: Throw MalformedFrameException (or another IOException subtype) for over-long declared lengths so that all wire-format rejections leave the decoder through one, declared, handled channel.

findings.title: Table decoding loop is driven by available(), which silently truncates instead of failing
findings.impact: Where the underlying stream is not fully buffered, a table or array decodes as a valid, complete value with trailing entries silently dropped, and the stream is left positioned mid-value, desynchronising every subsequent read. Silently losing headers is security-relevant when a header carries authorisation or routing context: the application sees a well-formed message that is missing a field it would have rejected on.
findings.evidence: readTable() loops `while(tableIn.available() > 0)` (line 148) and readArray() loops `while(arrayIn.available() > 0)` (line 244). InputStream.available() is defined as the bytes readable without blocking, not the bytes remaining, and returning 0 early is legal. The public constructor `ValueReader(DataInputStream in)` (line 57) accepts any DataInputStream and documents no requirement that it be fully buffered in memory; the declared tableLength (line 142) is used only to build the TruncatedInputStream, never to verify that exactly that many bytes were consumed.
findings.recommendation: Drive the loop from the declared length — track bytes consumed against tableLength/length and require the count to land exactly on the boundary — and throw MalformedFrameException on a short or over-long table instead of returning a partial one.

findings.title: Duplicate table keys resolve first-wins, creating a parser differential with the broker
findings.impact: Header smuggling. When a table carries the same field name twice, this client keeps the first occurrence while implementations that build the map by plain assignment keep the last. Any component that inspects or filters a header before the Java consumer sees it can therefore act on a different value than the consumer acts on, which defeats header-based filtering, tracing or authorisation checks.
findings.evidence: readTable() lines 151-152: `if(!table.containsKey(name)) table.put(name, value);` — the second and later values for a repeated name are discarded without any error, and the wire format places no uniqueness constraint on field names.
findings.recommendation: Reject duplicate field names with a MalformedFrameException rather than silently resolving them; if compatibility forbids that, document the first-wins rule explicitly as the library's ruling so integrators can align intermediate components.

findings.title: readTimestamp() silently overflows when converting seconds to milliseconds
findings.impact: A remote peer controls the sign and magnitude of the decoded Date independently of the value it put on the wire. Multiplying a 64-bit attacker-supplied value by 1000 wraps silently, so a very large positive timestamp can decode to a date in the past (and vice versa). Applications that use the AMQP timestamp for expiry, replay windows or ordering can be handed a timestamp that passes their freshness check while the wire value would not have.
findings.evidence: readTimestamp() line 269: `return new Date(in.readLong()*1000);`. `in.readLong()` is the raw wire value with no range check, and the multiplication is plain long arithmetic, which wraps rather than throwing for any magnitude above roughly 9.2e15.
findings.recommendation: Use Math.multiplyExact(seconds, 1000L) and convert the resulting ArithmeticException into a MalformedFrameException, or range-check the seconds value before converting.

findings.title: readTable() returns an immutable map for an empty table and a mutable one otherwise
findings.impact: The remote peer decides whether the map handed to application code is mutable. A consumer that enriches headers in place (a common pattern when republishing or forwarding) works on every message until a peer sends a zero-length table, at which point it fails with UnsupportedOperationException on a path that was never exercised in testing — a remotely triggerable crash in application code that the library's own contract gave no warning about.
findings.evidence: readTable() line 143: `if (tableLength == 0) return Collections.emptyMap();` while the normal path returns `new HashMap<String, Object>()` (line 145). Collections.emptyMap() is immutable; the HashMap is not. tableLength comes straight off the wire (line 142).
findings.recommendation: Return the same type on both paths — either `new HashMap<>()` for the empty case, or wrap the populated map with Collections.unmodifiableMap() and declare the return value immutable.

findings.title: Short strings are decoded with lenient UTF-8, so malformed keys collapse instead of being rejected
findings.impact: Distinct byte sequences on the wire can decode to the same String key. Combined with the first-wins rule (F-005), the later of two colliding entries is dropped without error, so what the application observes is not a faithful representation of what arrived.
findings.evidence: readShortstr() line 70: `return new String(b, "utf-8");`. This constructor replaces malformed and unmappable sequences with U+FFFD rather than signalling an error, and the decoded String is then used directly as the map key in readTable() (lines 149-152). The AMQP 0-9-1 grammar specifies shortstr as UTF-8, so invalid input is a protocol violation the decoder currently accepts.
findings.recommendation: Decode with a CharsetDecoder configured with CodingErrorAction.REPORT (StandardCharsets.UTF_8.newDecoder()) and convert a decoding failure into a MalformedFrameException.

findings.title: Compile-scope logging facade and several test dependencies sit on end-of-life release lines
findings.impact: These branches no longer receive fixes, so any future defect found in them has no upgrade path short of a major version bump. slf4j-api is the only one that reaches consumers of the published artifact (compile scope, no `optional` flag); the others affect only the build and test environment.
findings.evidence: pom.xml declares `<slf4j.version>1.7.36</slf4j.version>` (line 58, used at line 378 with default compile scope), `<logback.version>1.2.13</logback.version>` (line 64, test scope at line 439) and `<jetty.version>9.4.58.v20250814</jetty.version>` (line 70, test scope at line 457). The 1.7.x slf4j, 1.2.x logback and 9.4.x Jetty lines are all superseded maintenance branches, in contrast with the rest of the manifest, which tracks current releases (netty 4.2.15, jackson 2.21.3, bouncycastle 1.84, junit 5.14.4, mockito 5.23.0). No advisory lookup was performed for this engagement; this is a release-line maintenance judgement, not a claim that a specific vulnerability is present.
findings.recommendation: Plan the move of slf4j-api to the 2.x line (it stays Java 8 compatible) and of the test stack to maintained logback and Jetty branches, so a future fix does not require an emergency major upgrade.
